around Nunavik and bordering regions. We extracted various environmental variables 
109 
representing the different habitats occupied by Arctic Char and combined multiple gene-
110 
environment association methods to identify candidate SNPs associated with environmental 
111 
factors.  
112 
2. Methods 
113 
2.1 Sampling and DNA extraction 
114 
Arctic Chars were sampled in 23 water bodies across Nunavik, southern Baffin Island, 
115 
and Labrador (Figure 1). In Nunavik and Baffin Island, adult fish were harvested during their 
116 
upstream migration using gillnets or counting weirs. In most localities throughout Nunavik, 
117 
sampling locations were selected in concert with local and regional Inuit wildlife managers, and 
118 
sampling was done with the assistance of local Inuit guides, to prioritize fish populations with 
119 
an importance for traditional fishing. In two locations (Deception Bay and Hopes Advance Bay), 
120 
samples were taken in the estuary as well as in two tributary rivers. Juvenile fish were captured 
121 
by electrofishing in two rivers near Nain, Labrador. Adipose fin clips were collected from each 
122 
fish and preserved in ethanol 95%. DNA was extracted from fin clips using a modified version of 
123 
Aljanabi & Martinez (1997). Agarose gel electrophoresis was used to assess DNA quality and the 
124 
quantity and quality of DNA was evaluated by NanoDrop spectrophotometer (Thermo 
125 
Scientific). 
126 
2.2 Mitochondrial DNA analysis 
127 
Based on the analysis of mtDNA, Salisbury et al. (2019) showed an overlap of the Arctic 
128 
and Atlantic lineages in Northern Labrador (55 – 59° latitude), and an absence of correlation 
129 
.

between latitude and lineage prevalence which suggests a complete introgression of fish from 
130 
Arctic and Atlantic origins in the region. To assess whether the two glacial lineages also 
131 
hybridized in Nunavik, which could influence interpretations of nuclear diversity results, we 
132 
sequenced mtDNA for a subset of individuals from sampling sites in the eastern part of our 
133 
study area (n = 10 to 34 per site). The entire mitochondrial control region was amplified with 
134 
primers Tpro2 (Brunner et al., 2001) and SalpcrR (Power et al., 2009) and we sequenced 499 
135 
base pairs of the control region left domain region according to methods outlined in Power et 
136 
al. (2009). Control region sequences were aligned on the reference haplotype set described in 
137 
Salisbury et al. (2019) using the geneious (6.1.8; www.geneious.com) alignment tool with 
138 
parameters set to default and the closest matching haplotype was reported. 
139 
2.3 GBS library preparation, sequencing and SNP calling 
140 
Ten (10) µl of DNA samples were normalized to a concentration of 10 ng/µl using Quant-
141 
iT Picogreen dsDNA Assay Kit (Invitrogen) for precision quantification. GBS libraries were 
142 
prepared with a modified version of the Abed et al. (2019) two-enzyme GBS protocol, using PstI 
143 
and MspI restriction enzymes. Samples were randomly assigned to libraries to limit batch 
144 
effects. Sequencing was done on Ion Torrent p1v3 chips with a median target of 80 million 
145 
single-end reads per chip. Each library was sequenced on 3 separate chips, and the volume of 
146 
DNA from each sample was adjusted after the first chip to reduce the unbalanced 
147 
representation of individuals in sequences. 
148 
We processed the data and filtered the SNP dataset using a RADseq workflow 
149 
(https://github.com/enormandeau/stacks_workflow) built around STACKS 2.5 (Rochette, 
150 
Rivera-Colón & Catchen, 2019). Briefly, the sequences were trimmed at 80 bp and aligned on a 
151

Salvelinus sp. reference genome (ASM291031v2; NCBI RefSeq: GCF_002910315.2; Christensen 
152 
et al., 2018) using bwa mem (-k 19 -c 500 -O 0,0 -E 2,2 -T 0) in BWA-0.717 (r1188; Li & Durbin, 
153 
2009) and samtools view (-Sb -q 1 -F 4 -F 256 -F 2048) in samtools 1.8 (Li et al., 2009).  SNPs 
154 
were called on polymorphic genotypes with at least 4X coverage per sample (-m), present in at 
155 
least 60% of samples of each sampling sites (-r) and with the minor allele present in a minimum 
156 
of 3 samples. This minor allele sample (MAS) filter is akin to minor allele frequency (MAF), but 
157 
unlike MAF it is not artificially boosted by frequent RADseq genotyping errors (Linck & Battey, 
158

159 
removed. For SNP calling and quality control, we combined our samples with 119 other samples 
160 
from three sampling sites that weren’t included in our final dataset, as they either had too few 
161

162 
Salmonid fishes have a common ancestor that experienced a whole-genome duplication 
163 
approximately 60 MYA (Crête-Lafrenière, Weir & Bernatchez, 2012), and many genetic markers 
164 
identified in our analyses are expected to be situated on paralogous loci of similar sequences. 
165 
While these loci may be important for adaptation (Kondrashov, 2012), they were removed due 
166 
to the fact that these markers do not behave like bi-allelic SNPs and because genotyping is 
167 
difficult without very high coverage (>100 reads; Dufresne, Stift, Vergilino & Mable, 2014). SNPs 
168 
on duplicated loci were categorized and filtered using an adapted HDplot procedure (McKinney, 
169 
Waples, Seeb & Seeb, 2017), which identifies paralogs by visually comparing the allelic ratio, 
170

171 
SNP.

We also filtered the markers to avoid physically linked SNPs while keeping a maximum

considered linked and only the first SNP was kept. To identify markers linked to sex, we

2.4 Identification of putative neutral markers 
185 
Markers potentially under selection were identified using two methods: pcadapt (Luu, 
186 
Bazin & Blum, 2017) and BayeScan (Foll & Gaggiotti, 2008). SNPs identified as outliers by at 
187 
least one method were removed to produce a neutral dataset. The R package pcadapt identifies 
188

189

190 
recommended by pcadapt authors, and SNPs with minor allele frequencies under 0.05 were 
191 
excluded from the analysis. We then used BayeScan with prior odds of 1,000 and other 
192

4. Discussion 
413 
Anadromous salmonids are considered prime models for understanding local adaptation 
414 
(Fraser et al, 2011) and the many landscape genomics studies which they have been the subject 
415 
of have provided key information for the conservation and management of economically 
416 
important species (Waples, Naish & Primmer, 2020). Here, we documented for the first time 
417 
patterns of neutral and adaptive genetic variation in anadromous Arctic Char populations in the 
418 
Nunavik region using genomic data. By combining fine- and broad-scale sampling, our results 
419 
revealed a hierarchical genetic structure. Neighboring hydrographic systems generally harbored 
420 
distinct populations that could be regrouped within oceanographic basins, while differentiation 
421 
was also influenced by isolation-by-distance. To assess the potential for local adaptation to the 
422 
contrasted environments in our study area, we combined three GEA methods. By doing so, we 
423 
found genomic signatures that were consistent with local adaptation to either freshwater or 
424 
marine habitats. 
425

427 
most of the Hudson Bay and the Ungava Bay remained glaciated. By 6,500 – 7,200 YBP, the

4.2 Contemporary gene flow 
452 
Our results revealed a hierarchical genetic structure with most geographic regions 
453 
containing distinct populations of Arctic Char in every sampled river not sharing an estuary. 
454 
However, population structure in Hudson Bay appeared weaker, as there were signs of 
455

456 
attributed low genetic differentiation over long distances to recent post-glaciation colonization 
457 
events (Moore et al., 2013; O’Malley et al., 2019). However, lower salinity and a longer summer 
458 
period in Hudson Bay could also lead to higher connectivity between estuaries.  
459 
As migration in Arctic Char has been found to be predominantly coastal (Moore, 1975; 
460 
Moore et al., 2013, 2015; Spares et al., 2012), we expected the Hudson Strait, a 120-km-wide 
461 
open water area, to restrict gene flow between populations on opposite shores. However, 
462 
those pairs of populations did not deviate from IBD, which could suggest ongoing gene flow 
463 
over long marine stretches. In contrast, we did find limited evidence for Hudson Strait acting as 
464 
a barrier to gene flow at a finer spatial scale, i.e. by restricting analyses to sampling sites around 
465 
the strait. Differentiation between populations separated by the Hudson Strait was lower than, 
466 
for example, pairwise FST between populations in western and eastern Ungava Bay, despite 
467 
those populations being connected by a near-shore migration route. We cannot exclude the 
468 
possibility of other barriers to gene flow in our study area, as near-shore oceanographic 
469 
features could also limit dispersal (e.g., Quéméré et al., 2015), but differentiation in Ungava Bay 
470 
could also be driven by nuclear introgression from the Atlantic lineage in the eastern sampling

477 
Arctic Char is known for its higher straying rates than other salmonids, but many studies 
478 
argue that this dispersal does not necessarily lead to gene flow, as individuals are more prone 
479 
to straying when overwintering than when breeding (Moore et al., 2013; Moore et al. 2017; 
480 
Sévigny, Harris, Normandeau, Cayuela, Gilbert & Moore, in prep). In this study, adults sampled 
481 
in rivers sharing an estuary generally did not exhibit population structure, suggesting high levels 
482 
of straying between nearby rivers.  However, in a more surprising case, there was no signs of 
483 
adult dispersers between the Leaf River (FEU) and the Bérard River (BER), which also share an 
484 
estuary. Interestingly, those two rivers are on either side of the limit of two major geological 
485 
provinces (Thériaut & Beauséjour, 2012). As salmonids rely partly on their olfaction to recognize 
486 
their natal rivers (Keefer & Caudill, 2014), the distinct geologies of the Leaf and Bérard systems 
487 
could perhaps improve their homing ability and thus limit straying in these systems.  
488 
4.3 Genomic evidence for local adaptation 
489 
We explored how genetic variation in Arctic Char was linked to a range of climatic and 
490 
physical environmental predictors while considering both freshwater and marine habitats, 
491 
something that has rarely been done in salmonids (but see Bekkevold et al., 2019). While 
492 
different GEA methods identified candidate SNPs with every environmental component

495 
In our study, we treated the environment experienced by anadromous Arctic Char over 
496 
their life cycle as a complex set of collinear variables, hence leading to our inability to 
497 
differentiate signatures of selection in the freshwater and marine habitats. We also created two 
498 
sets of habitat-specific environmental components, but marine and freshwater components 
499 
were strongly correlated and created several instances of candidate SNPs associated to both a 
500 
marine and freshwater component by GEA methods (results not shown). Nevertheless, using 
501 
those habitat-specific components, we did find through a constrained ordination that both 
502 
habitats independently explained significant proportions of the genetic variation. For instance, 
503 
measures of air temperature (as a surrogate for river temperatures) and sea temperatures were 
504 
highly correlated, but likely caused selective pressures at different life stages. Several studies 
505 
have found temperature to be a driver of genetic structure and local adaptation in salmonids, 
506 
with most studies focusing on freshwater measures (Dionne et al., 2008; Bourret et al., 2013; 
507 
Perrier et al. 2017; Silvester et al. 2018). In contrast, selective pressures in marine habitats have 
508 
been argued to be weaker since observed mortality rates are lower at sea (Garcia de Leaniz et 
509 
al., 2007; Quinn, 2005). However, SST near the mouth of spawning river was found to be 
510 
correlated with timing of migration in species of Pacific salmon (Kovach, Ellison, Pyare & 
511 
Tallmon, 2015) and to phenology-related genes in Arctic Char (Madsen et al., 2019). Sampling 
512 
sites across our study area displayed considerably different SST conditions: while coastal waters 
513 
surrounding sampling sites in Hudson Bay reached mean summer SSTs ranging from 5.5 – 7.5°C, 
514 
Hudson Strait stayed closer to the freezing point (0.5 – 2°C). Such contrasts in surface

518 
Recent studies of local adaptation in salmonids have focused on tributary-specific 
519 
variation in freshwater conditions within a single catchment, (e.g., the Columbia River; Hand et 
520 
al., 2016; Hecht et al., 2015, Micheletti et al., 2018). However, the freshwater environmental 
521 
factors used in our study are catchment-based given our sampling strategy., which prevents us 
522 
from knowing the precise spawning site or overwintering lake. In marine systems, genomic 
523 
evidence for local adaptation and isolation-by-environment has been found both at local scales 
524 
in heterogeneous habitats (e.g., Lenhert et al., 2019; Miller et al., 2019) and over large 
525 
geographic distances (e.g., Clucas, Lou, Therkildsen & Kovach, 2019). Arctic Char is expected to 
526 
use preferred habitats based on temperature, salinity, and prey availability (Harris et al., 2020; 
527 
Spares et al., 2012; 2015). As we averaged near-shore marine conditions around river mouths, 
528 
this study is limited to broad-scale environmental heterogeneity. This is in line with the 
529 
suggestion by Fraser et al. (2011), that adaptation of anadromous salmonids to the marine 
530 
environment should occur at a larger spatial scale than in fresh water. 
531 
Regardless of the geographic scale being studied, an ideal sampling design for detecting 
532 
local adaptation should maximize the environmental variation while minimizing its collinearity 
533 
with neutral genetic patterns. For example, Lotterhos and Whitlock (2015) suggested sampling 
534 
pairs of populations with similar ancestry and contrasting environments. Such a design is 
535 
suitable when studying variables that may change drastically over short distances, such as 
536 
catchment area and upstream migration distances. However, climatic and physicochemical

4.4 Implications for conservation and management 
562 
Genomic data has the potential to improve the definition of management and 
563 
conservation units by accounting for neutral genetic structure as well as local adaptation 
564 
(Bernatchez et al., 2017; Funk et al., 2012). Arctic Char populations in Nunavik support 
565 
important small-scale subsistence fisheries, and stocks are managed on a river-by-river basis on 
566 
the premise that each river contains a single and distinct population (Johnson, 1980). However, 
567 
the very low genetic differentiation in rivers sharing an estuary and our inability to identify 
568 
substructure at this level suggest high levels of straying in adults, in line with the evidence for 
569 
the prevalence of mixed stocks of Arctic Char in adjacent rivers (Boguski, Gallagher, Howland & 
570 
Harris, 2016; Moore, Lewis & Tallman, 2014; Moore et al., 2017). If genomic tools were to be 
571 
used for stock assignment of adult fish (e.g., Meek et al., 2016; Moore et al. 2017), further local 
572 
sampling including juveniles and/or reproducing adults would be useful to better understand 
573 
fine-scale population structure. The evidence we found for local adaptation to environments is 
574 
in concordance with the neutral genetic structure at a broader scale, as major oceanographic 
575 
basins around Nunavik are contrasted both in their environments and ancestry of their Arctic 
576 
Char populations. We therefore suggest that these regional differences between Hudson Bay, 
577 
Hudson Strait, and Ungava Bay (with distinction of the western and eastern coast) should form 
578 
the basis of management actions at a regional level. 
579 
Also, there is growing interest in Arctic Char hatchery projects in Nunavik, both for 
580 
supplementation and reintroduction of Arctic Char in traditional fishing locations (George,

582

583

584

585

586 
As the Arctic warms at a greater pace than any other regions on earth (Cohen et al., 
587 
2014), there might be concern about the response of Arctic Char populations to their changing 
588 
environment. Traits that are currently optimally adaptive in the present environment could 
589 
eventually become maladaptive. Species will thus likely need to shift their distributions 
590 
poleward and/or will need to adapt in order to persist in their current distribution if there is 
591 
presence of appropriate genetic diversity/phenotypic plasticity. A temporal study recently 
592 
showed that Arctic Char populations in Greenland have exhibited stable genetic structure over 
593 
the last 60 years in face of rapid climate change, and argued that gene flow, although low, 
594 
could allow for a modest level of evolutionary rescue in the short term (Christensen, Jacobsen, 
595 
Nygaard & Hansen, 2018). Our study shows potential for local adaptation of Arctic Char 
596 
populations to both their marine and freshwater habitats. As changes in climate might operate 
597 
at a different pace, scale, and stability in marine and terrestrial ecosystems (Burrows et al., 
598 
2011), there is a need for continued research about the interaction of selective pressures over 
599 
the lifespan of anadromous organisms.

Figure Legends 
Figure 1: Sampling locations in Nunavik (Québec) and bordering regions. Red extents numbered 1 to 6 
are magnified to show neighboring sampling locations. Samples were either used for Genotyping-by-
Sequencing (GBS) only (round) or for GBS and mitochondrial DNA sequencing (square). Catchment area 
for each site is displayed in green.  
Figure 2: (A) Population structure assessed by a principal coordinate analysis (PCoA). Individual scores 
on PCoA axes 1 and 2 are presented as points and colored by a priori geographical region. An ellipse 
representing a 95% confidence interval was drawn around each sampling site. The percentage of genetic 
variance explained by each axis is in parentheses.  
Figure 3: (A) Results of the hierarchical Bayesian clustering analysis implemented in ADMIXTURE for a 
number of genetic clusters (K) of 4, 6 and 13. Lower rows display the results for separate analyses on 
sampling sites sharing similar membership to clusters at K = 13, which yielded the lowest cross-
validation error (CV). (B) Results of ADMIXTURE for K = 4 clusters, with individual ancestry averaged by 
sampling site and represented by pie charts. Approximative extent of glaciers, adapted from Dyke 
(2004), are represented by blue dashed lines for 6,000 - 11,000 years before present (BP). 
Figure 4: Individual proportion of heterozygous SNP markers in sampling sites, ordered following the 
coast from west to east, and colored by region. Sampling sites on connecting rivers and estuaries were 
grouped, except for FEU and BER. For each boxplot, bold line indicates mean, the box limits 25th and 75th 
percentile, and whiskers represent 10th and 90th percentile. Letters indicate group membership based on 
a comparison of least square means in a mixed-effect model (p < 0.05).  
Figure 5: (A) Pairwise FST between neighboring sampling sites are shown, with line thickness proportional 
to values. All pairwise FST values are presented in Table S3. Red extent is magnified to contrast FST
